# 1: Project Overview

In the Canadian Football League, 3rd down is the kind of play where if a team does not reach the line to gain, they turn the ball over to the other team. In response to the pressure, teams decide to punt the ball downfield, kick for a field goal, or take the risk and play the ball to get a first down. My project aims to help teams make better decisions in this scenario using play-by-play data from the 2024 and 2025 seasons so teams aren't just driven by fear, but also data.

## 2.2.1: CFL Charts PbP Data

**Producer and authority.** CFLCharts.ca is a third-party site using public play-by-play and other game information given by the CFL's API, with additional stats like win probabilities and expected points for valuing game situations. It is likely just a passionate fan publishing to share insights.

**Original Dataset Purpose.** Observing the site, it looks like just a passionate CFL fan with a data science background who wanted to expand on game data shared their findings. There's no public name on the site or the twitter page.

**Collection method.** The data is collected from the CFL API's play-by-play info. The data is not manually checked for accuracy.

**Coverage and resolution.** One row per recorded play. A single game dataset has 148 plays with 93 columns. The coverage being used is all of the 2024 season and a majority of the 2025 season.

**Licence.** Not found

**Access.** It was retrieved from cflcharts.ca, a website with a very simple interface. The base link is where the match data is accessed from. I accessed it Nov 18. Data stopped being posted on the site in September 2025, so it's reasonable to assume a chance that the site could come down without warning.

**Known problems.** The About section indicates a possibility of slightly inaccurate data. Also, EP and EPA statistics are not very clear on what exactly they are, although definitions can be found with clues and maybe some reverse engineering. Data is incomplete in that the 2025 season's data was not fully posted online, although datasets for each game are still available online. Another thing to be noted is the use of only one data source, although this could be considered a unique project, a problem with this one dataset that arises in the future could cause a big pivot prevented by a bigger group of sources.

## 2.3: Investigated and rejected sources

CFL Talk: PDFs were too time-consuming to extract data from, 15 page documents for each individual game with lots of buttons and dropdowns to press. Checked it out because it had up-to-date information but the info I can get elsewhere will do the job for this kind of work studying a general decision instead of game or player trends.

CFL API: Had problems documented online about moving APIs in 2023 and paywalls blocked in-depth data. No direct structured access to the new API could be established in an easy way. Checked it out because it is direct from the source and APIs have lots of potential to be helpful.


## 2.4: What I could not find

I could not find a full CSV collection for CFLcharts for the 2025 season and no bulk CSV download as that part of the site is "under construction" or something; i.e. likely abandoned. Explicit data license was also not found, and specifics on what the EP model within the data is.

## 3.2: Unresolved licensing 

I was unable to find a direct license for CFLcharts or the actual CFL API. I looked through the 'about', 'updates' and 'raw data' sections on the website, as well as every other tab and individual game sheet within the website. I looked outward and found the CFL terms of use, which allow use of their website contents for individual non-commercial and informational purposes only. It's unknown if any attribution is required but the site will be credited as well as where the data was derived from, as CFLcharts states "All data on CFLCharts.ca is sourced from the CFL's public facing API".

## 3.3: Downstream permissions

No open license offered for the combined (combining data for each game) dataset, due to unclear third-party redistribution rights. I can still offer a license for my code and written explanations.
I can offer an MIT License for my data scripts.
I can offer a CC BY type of license for open access to my analysis work.

# 4: Consent and identifiability

The statistics being used are public professional sports statistics, including information about clubs and players that are publicly identified in news publications and all other kinds of media. No private information is collected directly from any of the participants, all information is extracted live in front of crowds.

---

# 5: Exclusions and harms

## 5.1: Excluded data from the audit


Exclusions will only include a chunk of the 2025 season because of it not existing on the website. In turning the raw game datasets into one big table, there isn't any information at the moment that looks like it will need to be removed. Keeping the extra info will insure that if the EP and EPA statistics aren't figured out or don't prove useful, new statistics can be derived from the play data. The exclusion of part of the 2025 season could possibly impact the data by thinking of maybe teams started to make different decisions in situations as the season progressed over time and coaches got more comfortable or had more data to refer back to. Including the 2024 season as well ensures that there is a large sample size but also that atleast one full season cycle is accounted for in the case of possible changes over a season in strategy.

## 5.2: Who could be harmed

An inaccurate model or inaccurate results could paint players, coaches, clubs etc in bad lights and on a larger scale (if I were a highly accredited journalist or publication), jobs or contract terms could be impacted in both good and bad ways. Coaching decisions could be influenced in a misguiding way if outcome is faulty. Teams at lower levels and different leagues could also falsely apply conclusions to their own games and possibly earn negative game outcomes that impact athletes and staff.

## 5.3: Unreleased working data

I wouldn't exclude any working data if I didn't have to; i think it's a fairly important process of data transparency and organization to have raw script and data in your project files. I did an independent project where I gitignored a large raw data file because it was in the hundreds of megabytes and sometimes it's not super necessary if data wasn't excessively altered. In reference to that project I think I only added 2-3 columns to the original csv. I don't have a license to this data so I can't really release it but I wouldn't hide it on github for reproductive purposes, unless it was a big big file.

# 6: Data Stewardship

**Where it lives.** A repository on github. If I like how my project looks, I'll likely add it to my public group of projects with some modifications to prove that I am capable of some solid data analysis and coding work with reasonable AI help. I imagine it'll also be nice to look back on if I continue down my career path. 

**Who maintains it.** Likely nobody, unless I find a new passion in this final project and decide to add seasons and add more games as the league moves forward.

**Formats and dependencies.** In 2036, it's likely that the website hosting the original data would have been down for years, and maybe R itself (and then Rmd) could be out of date formats. I'm likely not using some complex packages unless I go through with a complex dashboard for data visualization. I could preserve it by documenting R package versions, having a strong README file, and preserving info on the original data sources, maybe dig into the original pdfs from the CFL for each game if I had an extra couple hours.

**Lifespan.** In sports, the timelines can get real messy. I think I wouldn't use 2023 season data or earlier, so the lifespan of conclusions from 2024-2025 would probably only stretch until 2027-2028 until it starts to be questioned. Or even earlier if there's a big revolution in play style or decision-making tendencies.
